rationale: I'm switching the Welch PSD from mean to median averaging across segments. The recordings have no artifact rejection, and ADHD subjects (mostly children) likely produce more blinks and movement, which add bursts of broadband and low-frequency power. A mean-averaged spectrum lets a few bad segments inflate delta/theta, which could hide or fake the theta/beta signal. The median keeps the typical background spectrum per channel.

I'm adding the per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each condition. It is the slope of a log-log line fitted to the Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, leaving out 7–14 Hz so the alpha peak doesn't bias it. Relative band power mixes the 1/f background with oscillatory peaks. A changed aperiodic slope, which reflects excitation/inhibition balance, has been reported in ADHD and may explain part of the theta/beta effect. The slope doesn't change with amplitude scale, which matters for the external datasets.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few eye-blink, movement or electrode-pop segments can dominate mean-averaged Welch spectra, especially in low frequencies where theta/delta sit. This change makes the spectral estimate robust by averaging 2 s Welch segments with the median instead of the mean, and it re-references to the common average so the relative-power topography doesn't depend on the amplifier's original reference (which also helps on the external datasets). I haven't run it, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few blink, movement or electrode-pop windows can dominate the mean-averaged Welch PSD. That inflates delta and beta power, which are exactly the bands behind the theta/beta ADHD marker. This change takes the median across Welch segments instead of the mean, so the spectral estimate resists transient artifacts. Everything else (relative log band power, standardization, L2 logistic regression) stays the same.

I'm adding one per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent to each condition, alongside the existing relative band powers. It's the slope of a log-log fit of the Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, with the 7–14 Hz alpha peak and the area near 50/60 Hz line noise left out of the fit. Part of what the theta/beta ratio picks up in ADHD may be a flatter or steeper broadband background rather than real oscillations. Because the slope doesn't change with amplitude scale, it should also hold up on external amplifiers.

I'm adding one aperiodic (1/f) exponent per channel and condition. It is fit as a straight line on log-power vs log-frequency over 2–7 Hz and 14–40 Hz, skipping the alpha peak. The exponent is thought to reflect cortical excitation/inhibition balance and differs in ADHD, partly overlapping the theta/beta ratio effect. It doesn't change if the signal is rescaled, which helps on external amplifiers. Relative band power alone mixes this background slope with oscillatory peaks.

Add a per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent to the relative band powers in both conditions. It is a robust log-log linear fit over 2–40 Hz that skips the 7–14 Hz alpha peak. ADHD has been linked to a flatter aperiodic slope (a change in excitation/inhibition balance), and part of the classic theta/beta effect may come from this slope. The exponent does not depend on amplitude scale, so it should hold up on external amplifiers.

I'm adding one new scale-invariant feature: the per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each condition. It is the slope of a log-log fit over 2–40 Hz, leaving out the alpha/beta-peak range (7–14 Hz). ADHD has been linked to a changed excitation/inhibition balance, which shows up as a flatter or steeper broadband slope. Relative band powers mix that slope with oscillatory peaks, so a linear model can't separate the two from the current features.

These are resting recordings with no artifact cleaning, so blinks, movement and electrode pops inflate the mean Welch periodogram. That hits delta/theta hardest (frontal, especially eyes-open), which contaminates the theta-related power that ADHD markers depend on. Switching Welch to a median over segments makes each spectrum robust to these occasional artifact windows without changing anything else.

I'm making the spectral estimate more robust. Each recording gets an average re-reference, then a Welch PSD that takes the median across 4-s segments instead of the mean. The recordings have no artifact rejection, so blinks, movement and electrode pops can inflate the mean-averaged band powers. The re-reference also makes the features less dependent on the original reference, which matters when the model is applied to external clinics. I haven't run this, so I don't know its Dev score yet; the current best is 0.774.

I'm switching Welch's per-segment averaging from the mean to the median (`average='median'`). The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few seconds of eye blinks or movement (especially in EO) can dominate the mean in delta/theta and distort the theta/beta-type relative powers. The median spectrum is robust to that contamination, independent of amplitude scale and recording length, and needs no thresholds to tune.

These recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few blink, movement or muscle segments can inflate the mean Welch spectrum. That mostly hits the delta and beta/gamma bands that the theta/beta-type ADHD markers depend on. Averaging the Welch segments with the median instead of the mean makes each subject's spectrum (and its relative band powers) robust to these outlier epochs, without changing the feature set or the classifier.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so the mean Welch average lets a few eye blinks or movement bursts inflate delta and theta power in specific epochs. Those are the bands ADHD markers like the theta/beta ratio depend on. This change uses the median across Welch segments (`average="median"`) instead, so each subject's spectrum reflects typical resting activity rather than a few artifact epochs. That should also hold up better on the external recordings. I haven't run this version, so I don't have a score for it yet.

I'm adding a per-channel aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each condition alongside the existing relative band powers. The exponent is fitted on log-log Welch spectra over 2–40 Hz, with the alpha peak (7–14 Hz) left out. A flatter or steeper 1/f slope is a proposed ADHD marker linked to the excitation/inhibition balance. It is not captured by relative band power, and it does not depend on amplitude scale, which should help it carry over to external datasets recorded on other amplifiers.

Recordings are not artifact-cleaned, so blinks, movement and electrode pops add large broadband bursts. These bursts inflate the mean-averaged Welch PSD, especially delta/theta in EO. That blurs the theta/beta-type differences that separate the groups. I'm switching only the PSD estimator to median-across-segments Welch (`average="median"`), which ignores rare artifact segments and keeps the background spectrum. I'm adding the aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each channel and condition, estimated from the same Welch spectrum. The fit is a straight line in log-log space over 2–40 Hz, leaving out 7–14 Hz so the alpha peak doesn't distort it. The aim is to separate broadband spectral steepness, which several papers report changes in ADHD and which may explain much of the theta/beta-ratio effect, from true band-limited oscillations. The slope does not depend on amplitude scale, which should help on external recordings. I haven't run this; the score will come from the harness.

That corrupts the theta and beta powers that carry the ADHD signal. I'm switching to a median across Welch segments, which ignores those transient artifacts and makes the band-power features more stable within and across recordings.

ADHD has been linked to a flatter (or otherwise changed) aperiodic slope. Eye blinks and muscle bursts in these minimally processed recordings would otherwise inflate delta and gamma power.
